title.en: The King and the Vetala: Twenty-Five Tales on a Corpse's Shoulders
title.zh: 王與毘舍遮：負屍肩上的二十五個故事

region.zh: 陀羅陀羅火葬地（象徵性定位）

texts.period: Kathasaritsagara of Somadeva, c. 1070 CE, Vetala-Panchavimshati cycle (Tawney translation, 1880-84)

source.work: The Katha Sarit Sagara, trans. C. H. Tawney (1880-84), the Vetala tales

summary.en: A king was asked by a mendicant to fetch a corpse from a burning ground for a rite - and the corpse was a vetala, a spirit who told stories. Twenty-five times the king carried it on his shoulders and twenty-five times a riddle at the end of the tale tempted an answer; twenty-five times the vetala flew back to the tree. The frame is the tradition's great logic-exam: answer correctly and be caught, or keep silence and be called a coward.
summary.zh: 一位苦行者請王赴火葬地取一具屍體以行其祭——而屍體乃一毘舍遮（起屍鬼），講故事的精靈。二十五次王以肩負屍，二十五次故事末尾的謎題誘其作答；二十五次毘舍遮飛返樹上。此框架是傳統的邏輯大考：答對則被擒，沉默則被斥為懦夫。

passages.text: The mendicant's request sounded simple: a corpse from the burning ground on the fourteenth night - and the king, a man of his word, went alone to the dark to keep it. The corpse spoke as it was lifted: stories to pass the road, riddles to break the bargain - and the rule was understood at once: speak the answer, and I fly back to the tree; keep silent, and be shamed as a coward. Twenty-five riddles later the king out-tricked the trickster - one question he answered with a truth so bare that the spirit stayed to be caught: the frame story is India's logic-classroom, and its diploma is a captured ghost.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Kathasaritsagara, Vetala cycle (Tawney 1880-84); not verbatim.

title.en: Three Suitors and the Girl Made of Bones, Ashes and Charms
title.zh: 三位求偶者與骨、灰、咒所成之女

region.zh: 鄔闍衍那火葬地（象徵性定位）

texts.period: Kathasaritsagara, Vetala-Panchavimshati tale, c. 1070 CE (Tawney translation, 1880-84)

source.work: The Katha Sarit Sagara, trans. C. H. Tawney (1880-84), Vetala tale of the restored maiden

summary.en: A maiden died and three suitors worked her three resurrections: one gathered her bones, one collected the ashes, one found the charm that restored her - and the restored girl was claimed by all three. The vetala asks the king: whose wife is she? The answer taught in the tale: the bones made the body she wears, but the one who knew the charm of life is the one who gave her back herself.
summary.zh: 少女已死，三位求婚者各完成其一部分的復活：一個收其骨，一個收其灰，一個尋得復原之咒——復生的少女被三者同時索求。毘舍遮問王：誰是她的丈夫？故事所教：骨成其所穿的身，而知生命之咒者才是把她還給她自己的人。

passages.text: The maiden was dead, and three men loved the fact back to life: the bones gathered, the ashes collected, the charm found - a resurrection in three trades. The girl stood restored and was claimed three times - by the builder of her body, the keeper of her dust, the caster of her life; the vetala's riddle is which claim is marriage. The king's answer - the one who gave her back to herself - sent the vetala flying, and the tale's logic stands: a body is not a wife; the self is what the charm restored.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Kathasaritsagara, Vetala tales (Tawney 1880-84); not verbatim.

title.en: The Bride Tested by the Serpent's Bite

texts.period: Kathasaritsagara, Vetala-Panchavimshati tale, c. 1070 CE (Tawney translation, 1880-84)

source.work: The Katha Sarit Sagara, trans. C. H. Tawney (1880-84), Vetala tale of the serpent-bite

summary.en: A bridegroom died of a serpent's bite on his wedding night; his bride, refused permission to burn with him, kept his body, caught the serpent as it returned to its hole, and held its head over her own neck - 'bite me or bring him back'. The serpent, out-bargained by a widow, restored the prince with its gift; the vetala's riddle asks who loved whom more - the wife who died for the husband, or the one who made death return him.
summary.zh: 新郎於婚夜死於蛇咬；其妻未獲准同焚，守其屍身，待蛇歸穴時將其擒住，以蛇首置於自己頸項——『咬死我，或使他復生』。蛇被寡婦逼出更好的交易，以其贈禮使王子復原；毘舍遮的謎題問誰愛得更深——為夫而死的新娘，還是令死亡歸還丈夫的那一位。

passages.text: The prince died on his wedding night, and the widow's petition to burn with him was refused - so she took the law of grief into her own hands. She caught the serpent at its hole and gave it her own neck as its next bite: bring him back, or take me instead - the bargain a snake could not refuse.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Kathasaritsagara, Vetala tales (Tawney 1880-84); not verbatim.

passages.text: The prince woke in her arms; the vetala asked the king to weigh two loves - the one who lay down under the fangs, the one who lay down under the law - and the answer was neither: the serpent's gift was the marriage.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Kathasaritsagara, Vetala tales (Tawney 1880-84); not verbatim.

title.en: The Sage and the Brazen门 Gate of Heaven's Gift

source.work: The Katha Sarit Sagara, trans. C. H. Tawney (1880-84), the sage and the heavenly gift

summary.en: A seer's hospitality was rewarded by heaven with a golden gate that gave whatever was asked at it - and the seer's city grew rich on the gift while his wife grew suspicious of the crowd. When the king of the city coveted the gate, the seer asked the gate to take itself away: prosperity that invites greed is a gift that must be declined. The vetala-style moral: the best gifts are the ones that can leave.
summary.zh: 仙人殷勤待客，上天以一扇金門為報——凡於門前所求皆得——而其城因禮而富，其妻卻因人潮生疑。當城王覬覦此門，仙人求門自去：招引貪婪的繁榮必須謝絕。毘舍遮式的道德：最好的禮物是能夠離開的。

passages.text: Heaven's reward for the seer's open door was a gate with an open hand: ask and it is given - and the poor of the district arrived before the rumor did. The king heard of it as a treasury and came with soldiers; the seer heard of it as a test and came with a sentence - a gift that breeds robbery is a curse wearing a crown. He asked the gate to leave, and it folded itself out of the world: the tale's arithmetic is bhakti's - abundance is only dharma when it can be closed.

title.en: Naravahanadatta and the Quest for the Vidyadhara Crown
title.zh: 那羅婆訶那達陀與飛天王冠之探索

region.en: Vindhya and Himalaya, Vidyadhara realms (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 溫迪亞與喜馬拉雅，飛天境域（象徵性定位）

texts.period: Kathasaritsagara of Somadeva, c. 1070 CE (Tawney translation, 1880-84)

source.work: The Katha Sarit Sagara, trans. C. H. Tawney (1880-84), the Naravahanadatta cycle

summary.en: The Ocean of Story's great frame: a prince told at birth that he will wear the crown of the Vidyadharas - the wizard-kings of the air - spends his whole youth on a quest up the mountains: sorcerers, flying cities, wife-captures, magic battles and loves, each one a story that contains another. The crown is less an object than the tale's own way of never ending.
summary.zh: 《故事海》的大框架：一個生來即被告知將戴飛天王冠——空中巫王之冠——的王子，終其青春在群山間探索：巫師、飛城、奪妻、魔戰與情愛，每一段皆為一個包含另一個的故事。王冠與其說是物，不如說是故事自身永不終結的方式。

passages.text: The prophecy was read at the prince's naming: this child shall wear the crown of the Vidyadharas - and the prophecy became the book's spine, every episode a step up the mountain. The quest's inventory reads like a carnival of the imagination: flying palaces, wives won in dream and war, sorcerer-duels, feasts where the guests are not human - the crown at the top and the story content to climb. Somadeva's point is structural: a tale that promises an ending can afford to delay it forever - the crown is the ocean's horizon, and the waves are the tales.

title.en: Gunadhya Burns His Book and the God Laughs
title.zh: 貢那陀耶焚其書而神笑

region.zh: 溫迪亞林中（象徵性定位）

source.work: The Katha Sarit Sagara, trans. C. H. Tawney (1880-84), Kathamukha, Gunadhya's burning

summary.en: Cursed into a demon's body, the sage Gunadhya wrote his great story-book in the language of beasts - Paiśachi - and no court would read it. Despairing, he began to burn his manuscript leaf by leaf; a king's men rescued seven chapters from the fire, read one aloud at a feast, and Shiva - who had given the world stories as a gift and seen them refused - laughed, and restored the sage. The Ocean of Story claims descent from those seven salvaged chapters.
summary.zh: 被詛咒入惡魔之身的仙人貢那陀耶以獸語（畢沙奇語）寫成其巨著，而宮廷無人肯讀。絕望中他開始逐葉焚毀手稿；一位王的臣僕自火中搶救出七章，於宴會上誦讀其一，濕婆——曾以故事為贈而見其被拒的神——大笑，復原了仙人。《故事海》自承源於那七章。

passages.text: The demon's book was written in the market language of goblins - brilliant, and unreadable to the Sanskrit courts it was offered to; rejection was the demon's second curse. He fed the manuscript to the fire leaf by leaf, a funeral for his own life's work - and the men who rescued seven chapters from the smoke rescued the tradition's ancestry with them.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Kathasaritsagara, Kathamukha (Tawney 1880-84); not verbatim.

passages.text: One chapter read at a feast fetched the king who read, and the god who had made stories out of his own smile laughed in approval: the sage was restored, the language forgiven, and the Ocean of Story began as a salvage-operation.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Kathasaritsagara, Kathamukha (Tawney 1880-84); not verbatim.

title.en: The Prince Who Trusted a Serpent and a Parrot

source.work: The Katha Sarit Sagara, trans. C. H. Tawney (1880-84), Vetala tale of the prince and the serpent

summary.en: Exiled by astrologers' warnings, a prince took shelter with a serpent and a parrot - the two creatures nobody trusts - and was betrayed by the humans he did trust. His serpent friend gave its fang-gift, his parrot flew reconnaissance, and the betrayal was paid back with interest; the vetala's riddle: which adviser was the true one? Answer: the ones without hands to take bribes.
summary.zh: 被占星師的警告所放逐的一位王子，寄身於蛇與鸚鵡之間——兩種最不被信任的生靈——卻被他信任的人類背叛。蛇友贈其毒牙之禮，鸚鵡為其偵察，背叛以利息償還；毘舍遮的謎題：誰是真正的謀士？答：沒有手可以受賄的那些。

passages.text: The astrologers' verdict cost the prince his kingdom; the creatures who sheltered him in the wild had no reason to flatter and no hands to pay - a serpent and a parrot. The humans who did shelter him sold him for gold; the serpent's venom and the parrot's wings undid the sale, and the thief paid what the astrologers had feared. The vetala's question - which counsel was true? - gets the king's answer and the tale's moral: advice without interest is the only kind worth taking; the rest is commerce with fangs.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Kathasaritsagara, Vetala tales (Tawney 1880-84); not verbatim.

title.en: Ratnaprabha, the Bride of the Flying City
title.zh: 羅陀那普羅婆：飛城之新娘

region.en: Vidyadhara city in the air (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 空中飛天之城（象徵性定位）

texts.period: Kathasaritsagara of Somadeva, c. 1070 CE (Tawney translation, 1880-84)

source.work: The Katha Sarit Sagara, trans. C. H. Tawney (1880-84), Ratnaprabha episode

summary.en: The Naravahanadatta cycle's love-stories are the Ocean of Story's romances of the air: a prince carried to a flying city, a bride who tests him with three tasks, a sorcerer-antagonist turned ally by courtesy. Ratnaprabha's marriage is the cycle's model: the Vidyadhara worlds marry mortals when courage and wit outweigh the wings - and the crown at the story's end is worn by a couple, not a king.
summary.zh: 那羅婆訶那達陀循環的愛情故事是《故事海》的空中羅曼史：王子被攜至飛城，新娘以三重任務試探他，術士對手因禮數而化為盟友。羅陀那普羅婆之婚是循環的典範：當勇氣與機智勝過羽翼時，飛天世界便與凡人聯姻——而故事末端的王冠由一對夫婦所戴，非一位君王。

passages.text: The flying city was a real address in the cycle's cosmology: reached by chariot, cloud or courage - and its princesses chose mortals by task rather than by gift. Ratnaprabha's three tests were a syllabus in loyalty: keep a secret in a treasury of wonders, hold a trust through a war of wizards, and ask for nothing - the marriage followed the exam. The crown of the Vidyadharas, promised at his birth, is won in these episodes as a shared thing: the epic of the air keeps insisting that its thrones are two-seated.
